screens.title: Limits of Key-Based Queries
screens.narratorSegment: Start by recognizing the scope and limitations of key-based access patterns. GetState gives you direct reads by primary key. GetStateByPartialCompositeKey lets you list keys that share a structured prefix. Both are efficient because they rely on lexicographic or exact key lookup. But they are not designed for filtering on arbitrary fields inside a JSON document. For example, finding all assets owned by "Alice" with a value greater than 1000, or orders placed within a date range, would require scanning many keys and doing field-level filtering inside chaincode. That approach is expensive because it moves filtering work from the index to the application layer and grows linearly with ledger size. A common misconception is to try to encode every searchable field into composite keys; while workable for a few predictable patterns, it quickly becomes brittle and combinatorial when queries combine multiple optional fields. The practical takeaway is this: use key-based methods for direct lookups and predictable range patterns, and turn to CouchDB rich queries when you need flexible, multi-field filtering. Ask yourself which side should do the heavy lifting — the database via indexes, or chaincode via in-memory filtering?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Limits of Key-Based Queries
Definition
Key-based lookups retrieve documents by primary key or structured key prefixes. They are efficient but cannot express arbitrary JSON field conditions.
Example: GetState("car123") returns a single car by key.
Example: GetStateByPartialCompositeKey("owner~make", "Alice") lists keys that start with the composite prefix.
Misconception: Encoding every searchable attribute into keys scales poorly and becomes inflexible.
Concrete scenario
You need all cars owned by Alice with year >= 2018. Without a JSON query engine you'd scan many keys and filter in chaincode.
Why it matters: scanning large ledgers in chaincode is slow and wastes compute during endorsement.
Key Takeaway: pick database-side queries when filters target document fields, not just keys.

screens.title: CouchDB as the World State
screens.narratorSegment: CouchDB can be configured as Fabric peers' world state database. When enabled, each ledger key maps to a JSON document in CouchDB. That document holds the asset fields your chaincode writes, like owner, year, and nested records. The important consequence is that CouchDB understands document fields: it can evaluate selectors that mention those fields directly. Fabric handles persisting documents and managing state updates; your chaincode simply reads and writes JSON as before. Remember that CouchDB used as world state is not a general-purpose external database for application logic — Fabric still exercises control over transactional updates. A common contrast to note: LevelDB stores binary key-values and does not support field-level JSON queries. Therefore if you need Mango queries, ensure your peers use CouchDB. An operational detail worth knowing is that Fabric will push index definitions from chaincode packages into CouchDB when those index files exist under META-INF. That makes index deployment repeatable and tied to your chaincode lifecycle. Reflect on whether your application needs flexible filters and reporting; if so, CouchDB as the world state is the enabling piece. CouchDB as the World State means with couchdb, fabric stores documents as json and allows mango selectors to query document fields directly, unlike leveldb.. In practical terms, how couchdb stores json documents for fabric peers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › CouchDB as the World State
What it means
CouchDB keeps each ledger key as a JSON document and supports JSON queries over those documents.
Document model
Fields you write in chaincode are queryable as JSON properties. Nested objects and arrays are preserved.
Example: A Car document with owner and year can be filtered by owner and numeric comparisons on year.
Operational note
To use Mango queries, peers must be configured with CouchDB. Index files in META-INF are automatically installed into CouchDB at chaincode deploy.
Why it matters: this makes advanced queries part of the chaincode lifecycle and reproducible across environments.

screens.title: Mango Query Structure
screens.narratorSegment: A Mango query is a JSON object centered on the selector key. The selector describes the conditions documents must satisfy. Common operators include $gt, $gte, $lt, $lte for numeric and date comparisons, $eq for equality, and logical combinations can be expressed by including fields inside the same selector object (implicitly AND) or by using $and and $or arrays when needed. For example {"selector":{"owner":"Alice","year":{"$gte":2018}}} finds documents where owner equals Alice and year is at least 2018. It's crucial to produce valid JSON and escape embedded strings correctly when you build the query string inside chaincode. A frequent error is placing conditions outside the selector object or constructing syntactically invalid JSON, which causes GetQueryResult to fail. Another nuance: Mango selectors can include nested fields using dot notation when documents include sub-objects. The main teaching point is to think of selector as the filter expression and to test your selectors interactively against CouchDB or with small datasets before embedding them in production chaincode. Mango Query Structure means mango queries use a selector json. multiple fields in selector are anded; use $gte, $gt, $lt, $lte and logical operators for range and combination queries.. In practical terms, selectors, operators, and json syntax for queries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Selector anatomy
Selectors are JSON objects that define which documents to return. Multiple fields in the same selector imply AND.
Operator examples: $gt, $gte, $lt, $lte, $eq
Logical composition: $and, $or for complex boolean logic
Concrete example
{
  "selector": {
    "owner": "Alice",
    "year": {"$gte": 2018}
  }
}
Tip: Test this selector against a small dataset. If you build it dynamically in Go, ensure string values are escaped and numeric values stay numeric.

screens.title: Using stub.GetQueryResult in Chaincode (Cars example)
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a compact Go example that queries cars owned by an owner and with a minimum year. The chaincode constructs a Mango JSON string using fmt. Sprintf to insert the owner and numeric bounds, then calls ctx. GetStub(). GetQueryResult. The returned iterator must be closed with defer to release resources. For each result, call Next on the iterator, check the error, and unmarshal the Value into your Car struct. A common pitfall is trying to unmarshal the Key instead of Value, or failing to defer Close which leaks resources. Another is building the selector as an unescaped string and allowing injection-like issues; prefer validated inputs and escaping where needed. Finally, remember that GetQueryResult returns documents based on CouchDB indexes — without matching indexes the query will trigger a full database scan, which will be slow. This example demonstrates correct iterator handling, error propagation, and robust unmarshaling so endorsing peers remain stable under load. keyIdea.title: Iterator pattern
keyIdea.text: Call GetQueryResult with a valid selector string, defer Close on the iterator, iterate with HasNext/Next, and unmarshal result.Value into your struct.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › GetQueryResult Walkthrough
Key code pattern
queryString := fmt.Sprintf(`{"selector":{"owner":"%s","year":{"$gte":%d}}}`, owner, minYear)
resultsIterator, err := ctx.GetStub().GetQueryResult(queryString)
if err != nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to get query result: %v", err) }
defer resultsIterator.Close()
for resultsIterator.HasNext() {
  queryResponse, err := resultsIterator.Next()
  if err != nil { return nil, err }
  var car Car
  err = json.Unmarshal(queryResponse.Value, &car)
  if err != nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to unmarshal car: %v", err) }
  cars = append(cars, &car)
}
This pattern ensures resources are freed and each returned document is turned into a typed object for downstream logic.
Example pitfalls
  • Forgetting defer Close and leaking iterators.
  • Unescaping or misformatting the selector JSON string.
  • Relying on unindexed fields and suffering full scans.
Key Takeaway: iterator safety and valid JSON selectors are essential for reliable rich queries.

screens.title: Vehicle Rental: QueryVehicles Implementation
screens.narratorSegment: The vehicle rental example shows how to construct a Mango query dynamically when parameters may be optional. Start by initializing a selector string with an opening selector object. For each non-empty parameter—make, model, year, status—append a condition to a conditions slice. If the slice is empty, the query should be a select-all expression, {"selector":{}}. Otherwise join conditions with commas and close the selector. Print the query for debugging during development. Then call GetQueryResult and unmarshal results like before. A useful practice is to treat numeric zero values specially so they don’t become part of the selector when optional. Also validate client input: do not allow untrusted raw JSON to be concatenated into selectors without validation. Another practical point is logging the final query string during tests so you can confirm which index should be used. This dynamic construction pattern gives you flexible APIs: clients can pass a subset of filters and the chaincode builds an efficient query accordingly. Vehicle Rental: QueryVehicles Implementation means build selector conditions only for provided parameters, default to selector empty to query all, and avoid inserting invalid json by validating inputs.. In practical terms, building a dynamic selector from optional parameters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › QueryVehicles Implementation
Core pattern (excerpt)
conditions := []string{}
if make != "" { conditions = append(conditions, fmt.Sprintf(`"make":"%s"`, make)) }
if model != "" { conditions = append(conditions, fmt.Sprintf(`"model":"%s"`, model)) }
if year != 0 { conditions = append(conditions, fmt.Sprintf(`"year":%d`, year)) }
if status != "" { conditions = append(conditions, fmt.Sprintf(`"availabilityStatus":"%s"`, status)) }
if len(conditions) == 0 {
  queryString = `{ "selector": {} }`
} else {
  queryString = `{ "selector": {` + strings.Join(conditions, ",") + `}}`
}
This approach builds minimal selectors and avoids unnecessary conditions that would prevent index usage.
Practical checks
  • Log queryString during testing to validate structure.
  • Treat zero values as absent for optional numeric fields.
  • Validate string inputs to avoid malformed JSON selectors.
Key Takeaway: dynamic selectors make APIs flexible while keeping queries index-friendly.

screens.title: Custom Indexes for Performance
screens.narratorSegment: Indexes are the single most important optimization for CouchDB rich queries. Define a JSON index that lists the fields you query frequently and place the file in META-INF/statedb/couchdb/indexes inside your chaincode package. A compound index has ordered fields, and CouchDB uses the leftmost prefix of that order. That means an index on ["owner","year"] supports queries that include owner and year, but it may not efficiently support queries on year only. A common mistake is to forget to include indexes and then wonder why queries are slow; CouchDB will perform a full scan without a matching index. Another mistake is using an incorrect field order in compound indexes so CouchDB cannot apply the index in the expected cases. When designing indexes, list the most selective and most commonly used fields first. Finally, name your index and provide a ddoc string; Fabric will push these definitions to CouchDB when you deploy the chaincode package that contains them. Custom Indexes for Performance means create json index files listing fields in the correct order; place them under meta-inf so fabric deploys them and couchdb can use them for fast queries.. In practical terms, why indexes matter and how to define them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: GetQueryResult vs GetStateByRange
screens.narratorSegment: Fabric provides multiple read APIs and picking the right one matters. GetStateByRange is lexicographic and works best when your primary keys encode sortable attributes or when you perform predictable prefix scans. It’s inexpensive when the key structure matches your access pattern. In contrast, GetQueryResult with CouchDB executes Mango selectors that operate on JSON document fields, not keys. Use GetQueryResult when you need filters across arbitrary fields such as owner, category, or numeric ranges on non-key attributes. A common confusion is trying to force all searches into GetStateByRange by inventing composite keys — this can produce brittle key schemes and exponential growth in key combinations. Another important contrast is indexing: GetStateByRange relies on key ordering, whereas GetQueryResult needs CouchDB indexes defined for field-based queries. If you need both fast prefix lookups and flexible field filters, design your keys for frequent lookups and use CouchDB indexes for flexible reporting queries. GetQueryResult vs GetStateByRange means use getstatebyrange for lexicographic key scans and getqueryresult for flexible json field queries backed by couchdb indexes.. In practical terms, choose the right api for your query pattern. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Testing Queries and Diagnosing Slow Performance
screens.narratorSegment: When queries are slow, the first hypothesis should be missing or mismatched indexes. Start by logging the Mango query string produced by your chaincode during test runs. Then run the same selector directly against CouchDB or use Fabric peer logs to observe whether CouchDB performs a full table scan. If a query is slow and your index exists, check that the index fields match the selector fields and that the compound index order allows the query to use it. For example an index on ["owner","year"] supports queries that specify owner and year, but a query only on year likely won’t use that index. Another debugging step is to reduce the dataset and run the selector to confirm correctness and isolate performance scaling. Common operational mistakes include packaging index files in the wrong path or forgetting to redeploy the chaincode package after adding indexes. Finally, measure query times before and after index deployment to quantify the improvement. screens.title: Consistency and Operational Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Keep in mind that CouchDB provides eventual consistency semantics for indexes and views. Fabric still ensures ledger consistency through its ordering and endorsement model, but if your application reads directly from CouchDB outside of Fabric's transaction flow you may observe eventual consistency issues. The recommended pattern is to perform queries within chaincode during transactions so Fabric manages state transitions. Also be mindful of resource usage: complex queries that scan many documents can be resource intensive on peers; design queries and indexes to minimize scans. Avoid relying on CouchDB for operations that must be strongly consistent outside Fabric. Finally, treat index files, query patterns, and tests as part of your deployment artifact. Version your index JSON files with chaincode releases and include them in CI tests that run queries to validate both correctness and performance. This operational hygiene reduces surprises in production when datasets grow. fullNarratorScript:
In distributed ledger applications we often outgrow simple key lookups. This lesson shows how Fabric leverages CouchDB to store world state as JSON documents and how chaincode can execute Mango queries through the stub. GetQueryResult A P I. You will learn the structure of a Mango selector, how to construct query strings safely inside Go chaincode, and why custom JSON indexes are critical to query performance. We’ll also look at a practical vehicle rental example that builds flexible search over Make, Model, Year and AvailabilityStatus, plus the index file you must include in META-INF so Fabric pushes it to CouchDB at deploy time. Along the way I’ll highlight common mistakes: running rich queries without indexes, misunderstanding compound index ordering, and confusing GetQueryResult with key-range lookups. By the end you’ll see when to choose rich JSON queries and how to make them fast and maintainable. Think of this chapter as the bridge between ledger design and practical reporting: it gives you the tools to ask the world state useful questions without scanning the entire ledger.

In this first objectives slide we set four concrete learning goals. First, you will understand why key-based queries such as GetState or GetStateByPartialCompositeKey are limited when you need multi-field filters or range checks on non-key fields. Second, you will be able to explain how CouchDB stores world state as JSON documents and why that enables Mango queries — a JSON query language that runs inside CouchDB. Third, you'll learn to write and execute Mango queries from chaincode using stub. GetQueryResult, including constructing valid selector JSON and handling the results iterator safely. Fourth, you will understand the role of custom indexes: how to define index JSON files, why compound index field order matters, and how to place index files under META-INF/statedb/couchdb/indexes so Fabric deploys them. Each objective is competency-focused so you can validate the skill in a lab scenario. For example, after this chapter you should be able to add an index file to a chaincode package and observe significantly faster query performance for a targeted selector versus an unindexed full scan.

This second objectives slide focuses on applied skills and lab-ready tasks. You should be able to implement a chaincode function that builds a Mango query string dynamically based on optional parameters and safely passes it to stub. GetQueryResult. You will practice handling the results iterator correctly, closing it in a defer, and unmarshaling JSON documents into Go structs. You’ll also learn to author an index JSON file that lists fields in the correct compound order and include it in the META-INF/statedb/couchdb/indexes path of the chaincode package so Fabric deploys it automatically. Finally, you should be comfortable testing queries using peer chaincode query commands with different parameter combinations and observing the performance improvement after index deployment. These applied objectives let you demonstrate that rich queries are not just syntactic sugar — they are a repeatable, testable part of an efficient Fabric application.

Start by recognizing the scope and limitations of key-based access patterns. GetState gives you direct reads by primary key. GetStateByPartialCompositeKey lets you list keys that share a structured prefix. Both are efficient because they rely on lexicographic or exact key lookup. But they are not designed for filtering on arbitrary fields inside a JSON document. For example, finding all assets owned by "Alice" with a value greater than 1000, or orders placed within a date range, would require scanning many keys and doing field-level filtering inside chaincode. That approach is expensive because it moves filtering work from the index to the application layer and grows linearly with ledger size. A common misconception is to try to encode every searchable field into composite keys; while workable for a few predictable patterns, it quickly becomes brittle and combinatorial when queries combine multiple optional fields. The practical takeaway is this: use key-based methods for direct lookups and predictable range patterns, and turn to CouchDB rich queries when you need flexible, multi-field filtering. Ask yourself which side should do the heavy lifting — the database via indexes, or chaincode via in-memory filtering?

CouchDB can be configured as Fabric peers' world state database. When enabled, each ledger key maps to a JSON document in CouchDB. That document holds the asset fields your chaincode writes, like owner, year, and nested records. The important consequence is that CouchDB understands document fields: it can evaluate selectors that mention those fields directly. Fabric handles persisting documents and managing state updates; your chaincode simply reads and writes JSON as before. Remember that CouchDB used as world state is not a general-purpose external database for application logic — Fabric still exercises control over transactional updates. A common contrast to note: LevelDB stores binary key-values and does not support field-level JSON queries. Therefore if you need Mango queries, ensure your peers use CouchDB. An operational detail worth knowing is that Fabric will push index definitions from chaincode packages into CouchDB when those index files exist under META-INF. That makes index deployment repeatable and tied to your chaincode lifecycle. Reflect on whether your application needs flexible filters and reporting; if so, CouchDB as the world state is the enabling piece. CouchDB as the World State means with couchdb, fabric stores documents as json and allows mango selectors to query document fields directly, unlike leveldb.. In practical terms, how couchdb stores json documents for fabric peers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A Mango query is a JSON object centered on the selector key. The selector describes the conditions documents must satisfy. Common operators include $gt, $gte, $lt, $lte for numeric and date comparisons, $eq for equality, and logical combinations can be expressed by including fields inside the same selector object (implicitly AND) or by using $and and $or arrays when needed. For example {"selector":{"owner":"Alice","year":{"$gte":2018}}} finds documents where owner equals Alice and year is at least 2018. It's crucial to produce valid JSON and escape embedded strings correctly when you build the query string inside chaincode. A frequent error is placing conditions outside the selector object or constructing syntactically invalid JSON, which causes GetQueryResult to fail. Another nuance: Mango selectors can include nested fields using dot notation when documents include sub-objects. The main teaching point is to think of selector as the filter expression and to test your selectors interactively against CouchDB or with small datasets before embedding them in production chaincode. Mango Query Structure means mango queries use a selector json. multiple fields in selector are anded; use $gte, $gt, $lt, $lte and logical operators for range and combination queries.. In practical terms, selectors, operators, and json syntax for queries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a compact Go example that queries cars owned by an owner and with a minimum year. The chaincode constructs a Mango JSON string using fmt. Sprintf to insert the owner and numeric bounds, then calls ctx. GetStub(). GetQueryResult. The returned iterator must be closed with defer to release resources. For each result, call Next on the iterator, check the error, and unmarshal the Value into your Car struct. A common pitfall is trying to unmarshal the Key instead of Value, or failing to defer Close which leaks resources. Another is building the selector as an unescaped string and allowing injection-like issues; prefer validated inputs and escaping where needed. Finally, remember that GetQueryResult returns documents based on CouchDB indexes — without matching indexes the query will trigger a full database scan, which will be slow. This example demonstrates correct iterator handling, error propagation, and robust unmarshaling so endorsing peers remain stable under load. Using stub.GetQueryResult in Chaincode (Cars example) means call getqueryresult with a valid selector string, defer close on the iterator, iterate with hasnext/next, and unmarshal result.value into your struct.. In practical terms, constructing the query string and iterating results safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Indexes are the single most important optimization for CouchDB rich queries. Define a JSON index that lists the fields you query frequently and place the file in META-INF/statedb/couchdb/indexes inside your chaincode package. A compound index has ordered fields, and CouchDB uses the leftmost prefix of that order. That means an index on ["owner","year"] supports queries that include owner and year, but it may not efficiently support queries on year only. A common mistake is to forget to include indexes and then wonder why queries are slow; CouchDB will perform a full scan without a matching index. Fabric provides multiple read APIs and picking the right one matters. GetStateByRange is lexicographic and works best when your primary keys encode sortable attributes or when you perform predictable prefix scans. It’s inexpensive when the key structure matches your access pattern. In contrast, GetQueryResult with CouchDB executes Mango selectors that operate on JSON document fields, not keys. Use GetQueryResult when you need filters across arbitrary fields such as owner, category, or numeric ranges on non-key attributes. A common confusion is trying to force all searches into GetStateByRange by inventing composite keys — this can produce brittle key schemes and exponential growth in key combinations. Keep in mind that CouchDB provides eventual consistency semantics for indexes and views. Fabric still ensures ledger consistency through its ordering and endorsement model, but if your application reads directly from CouchDB outside of Fabric's transaction flow you may observe eventual consistency issues.
